chunks: And from him, from Safwan, from Jamil ibn Darraj and Ibn Abi Najran, from Muhammad ibn Humran, all of them, from Isma'il al-Ju'fi, who said:

I went out, along with Muyassar and some of our companions, and Zurara said to us, 'Perform Hajj.' So we entered upon Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and said to him, 'May God perfect you, we intend to perform Hajj, and we are a group of novices (or all of us are novices), so what should we do?' He said, 'Perform Umrah.' When we went out, 'Abd al-Malik ibn A'yan arrived, and I said to him, 'Do you not wonder at Zurara? He told us to perform Hajj, and indeed Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) told us, "Perform Umrah."' 'Abd al-Malik ibn A'yan entered upon him and said to him, 'A group of your mawali were ordered by Zurara to perform Hajj on your behalf, and when they entered upon you, you ordered them to perform Umrah.' Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said, 'Each of them wants to hear it individually (for himself). Bring them back to me.' So we entered, and he said, 'Perform Hajj, for the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) performed Hajj.'

Do you not see these two reports, and that they included the command to the questioner to enter the state of Ihram with Umrah leading to Hajj? When he saw that this would lead to confusion and to criticism of those who were specifically associated with him from the distinguished among his companions, he said to them, 'Perform Hajj,' and this confirms what we mentioned, that entering the state of Ihram with both (Umrah and Hajj) and reciting the Talbiyah with both is superior.

key_terms.إِهْلَال: Entering the state of Ihram (ritual consecration)
key_terms.تَّلْبِيَة: Recitation of the Talbiyah (chant during Hajj/Umrah)
key_terms.زُرَارَة: Zurara, a prominent companion of the Imams
key_terms.صَرُورَة: Novice or beginner in religious rituals

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on performing Umrah versus Hajj for novices according to Imam al-Baqir (peace be upon him)?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the principle of *al-ibaha al-awwaliyya* (original permissibility) and the Imam's strategic use of *taqiyya* or contextual guidance to prevent *fasad* (confusion or criticism) among the elite companions. It highlights the scholarly distinction between the general command to perform Hajj and the specific, perhaps more immediate, instruction for Umrah, ultimately affirming the superiority of the Hajj pilgrimage as practiced by the Prophet. The narrative underscores the dynamic nature of fiqh rulings based on the social and political context of the time.
